A map of Western solid rocket motor suppliers in 2026: incumbents, new entrants, capacity expansions, and the interceptor and strike programs they supply.

Fabian Hoffmann, PhD

Picture: Northrop Grumman
Until recently, U.S. and European missile production relied on a small number of solid rocket motor manufacturers for both full-scale motors that power rocket artillery, interceptors, and ballistic missiles, and smaller boosters that accelerate cruise missiles. In the United States, the main suppliers included Aerojet Rocketdyne (now part of L3Harris) and Northrop Grumman. In Europe, the principal players were Norway’s Nammo and France-based Roxel.
Since 2022, several startups and scale-ups have emerged, seeking to diversify the North American and European solid rocket motor industrial base. Incumbents and new entrants alike have also invested heavily in new production facilities and motor designs, while establishing supply agreements at an accelerating pace. Whether these developments are actually diversifying the supplier base, however, depends on solid rocket motor qualification, the supply chains into which new suppliers are integrated, and the timelines for doing so.
This post maps the Western solid rocket motor supplier base, the missile systems each company supplies or targets, and the status of ongoing capacity expansions. It also examines how new suppliers enter the market and identifies major interceptor and strike missile programs that still depend on a single solid rocket motor supplier.

$1.6B Lockheed Order Sends PAC-3 MSE Rocket Motor Work to Northrop Grumman

Lockheed Martin placed a $1.6 billion order with Northrop Grumman for the dual-pulse solid rocket motors and ignition safety devices behind the PAC-3 MSE interceptor, scaling production at Allegany Ballistics Laboratory as the Army looks to grow output from about 600 toward 2,000 missiles a year.
2026-11-19 · By Marcus Webb , AI-assisted desk · AI-drafted, source-checked, released by the publisher
Photo: U.S. Army photo by Capt. Frank Spatt, via Wikimedia Commons (public domain). A PAC-2 interceptor launch during Exercise Tenacious Archer 25, shown as a stand-in.

...

* Aviation and Missile R&D BAA Due Jul 3, 2029
* Sprra227r0702 Patriot Spares – Lockheed Martin Sole Source Due Jan 6, 2027
Rocket motors are a pacing item in the Army 's push to build far more Patriot interceptors, and Lockheed Martin has now put $1.6 billion behind the work at Rocket Center, W.Va. Northrop Grumman announced Nov. 16 that it is ramping production of solid rocket motors and essential components for the PAC-3 Missile Segment Enhancement (MSE) program under a new $1.6 billion order. The buyer is Lockheed Martin, the PAC-3 MSE prime, and the order covers the dual-pulse motors and ignition safety devices essential to Lockheed's production of PAC-3 MSE interceptors.
Northrop describes the work as a multi-year award and folds it into what it calls its "broader $3 billion landmark agreements announced in August". A company spokesperson told Defense Daily that Lockheed awarded the contract in mid-to-late October, weeks before the public announcement.

What the $1.6 Billion PAC-3 MSE Order Buys

The order pays for two things: the dual-pulse solid rocket motor that propels the PAC-3 MSE, and the ignition safety devices that go with it. Northrop's Allegany Ballistics Laboratory (ABL) in Rocket Center manufactures the motor, which the company says provides "maneuverability and extended range to counter evolving threats."
The spokesperson told Defense Daily that early production under the contract has already started and that the work is expected to last at least through the current seven-year framework agreement between Lockheed Martin and the Pentagon. Northrop declined to disclose how many motors it plans to build during the ramp. The spokesperson called the planned ramp "significant" and said it will support the Army's anticipated growth in annual PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 units to thousands "in the near term."
Lockheed had already signaled the order. On its Oct. 25 quarterly earnings call, CEO Jim Taiclet said that since the quarter closed the company had awarded a "$1.6 billion contract to Northrop Grumman for propulsion and other missile components", according to Defense Daily.

How the Northrop Award Fits the PAC-3 Production Surge

Defense Daily describes the Northrop order as a downstream effect of the Defense Department's framework agreements to expand production of the interceptor, and it lays out the sequence:
* In January, Lockheed Martin and the Defense Department signed a seven-year framework agreement aimed at raising annual PAC-3 MSE production from about 600 to 2,000 interceptors.

Solid rocket motors: the munitions bottleneck is drawing new builders

By Fluxa First
Table of solid rocket motor capacity moves in October 2026, including Ursa Major's $137 million Navy awards, X-Bow's Navy booster agreement, L3Harris's $250 million GMLRS follow-on and new Camden plant, and the Lockheed Martin and Avio agreement.

Key takeaways

* In October 2026 alone, L3Harris opened a Camden, Arkansas motor plant designed to double capacity and won a $250 million GMLRS follow-on that the company says is its highest quantity in program history.
* Lockheed Martin signed with Avio, whose US unit is building a Virginia plant as part of more than $500 million of US capacity investment.
* Newer companies also won Navy work, with Ursa Major receiving $137 million and X-Bow an agreement worth up to $69.7 million that includes tooling for a 500-motor-a-year line.
* More suppliers, merchant capacity and modern manufacturing make the propulsion base more resilient, and the bottleneck is now qualification and scale, not ideas.
Precision munitions and interceptors depend on a component most people never think about: the solid rocket motor. Demand has surged, and supply has struggled to keep up; X-Bow’s chief executive described it this month as a production bottleneck decades in the making. October 2026 showed how quickly that is changing. In a single month, an incumbent opened a new plant and won a record order, a European specialist signed with Lockheed Martin to build motors in Virginia, and two newer American companies won Navy contracts. For anyone watching the American industrial base, propulsion is where capacity is being rebuilt fastest.

What happened in October?

Table of October 2026 solid rocket motor moves: Ursa Major $137M Navy awards on Oct. 5, X-Bow Navy booster agreement worth up to $69.7M on Oct. 8, L3Harris $250M GMLRS follow-on on Oct. 12, Lockheed Martin and Avio agreement on Oct. 13, and L3Harris opening its Camden, Arkansas plant on Oct. 20.
* Ursa Major, October 5. The Navy awarded Ursa Major $137 million across two contracts: $91 million for a 7-inch motor for the Compact Air-to-Air Missile and $46 million for a 10-inch motor for the Naval Modular Missile. The company says both use its Lynx approach, combining expanded energetics capacity with additive manufacturing, and that the CAAM motor is being developed with the same methods planned for full production, while the NMM motor is designed for high-rate production.
* X-Bow Systems, October 8. X-Bow won a prototype agreement worth up to $69.7 million to develop and qualify a booster for a Navy next-generation weapon program, with $50 million obligated at award. It includes production-rate tooling at its Luling, Texas site, where it plans a line for up to 500 motors a year. X-Bow said it recently finished its first major production contract, delivering more than 2,100 motors.
* L3Harris, October 12. L3Harris received a $250 million follow-on from Lockheed Martin for standard-range GMLRS propulsion, the highest quantity in the program’s history, according to the company.
* Lockheed Martin and Avio, October 13. The two companies announced a cooperation agreement under which, after qualification, Avio USA’s new plant in Hurt, Virginia will produce motors for Extended Range GMLRS and the Precision Strike Missile. Avio says it is investing more than $500 million in US capacity to become a merchant supplier to several defense customers.
* L3Harris, October 20. L3Harris opened its Arsenal of Freedom plant in Camden, Arkansas, designed to double current GMLRS motor capacity with room to grow. It was built under a $216 million Defense Production Act Title III agreement signed in 2023, and the company says it is building about 60 new facilities across four states.

Why does this matter for sovereignty?

A country that cannot produce enough propulsion cannot sustain its own defense or support its allies. The same industrial skills, energetic materials, casting propellant, case manufacturing and testing, also matter for space launch and hypersonics. When only a few suppliers make a critical component, demand spikes are hard to absorb.

...

Making them requires energetic materials, specialized facilities, strict safety processes and long qualification. When demand surges, capacity limits show up quickly, which is why the Pentagon is funding new plants and new entrants.

What is a merchant supplier of solid rocket motors?

A merchant supplier sells motors to several prime contractors rather than building only for its own missiles. Avio says its US investment is aimed at becoming a merchant supplier to various defense customers, which gives primes more options and adds competition.

Taiwan's army reopens its NT$24.7m tender for night-vision and tethered drones after the first round stalled

The army posted a fresh tender on 24 November, seven months after the first, for drones that can watch over troops at night and stay aloft for hours on a cable.
T

Taipei · 25 Nov 2026, 02:57 TST
2 min read
X Facebook LinkedIn LINE
A grey four-armed multirotor drone on a camouflage-covered table in a hall, with a soldier in camouflage in the foreground and President Lai in a dark suit standing among officials behind it File photo: A soldier shows a multirotor drone to President Lai Ching-te during his visit to the army's Unmanned Systems Training Command in Tainan on 11 September 2026. Photo: Office of the President (Taiwan), CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) Liu Shu-fu, Office of the President, Republic of China (Taiwan) commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:09.11_%E7%B8%BD%E7%B5%B1%E5%8B%97%E5%8B%89%E9%99%B8%E8%BB%8D%E7%84%A1%E4%BA%BA%E7%B3%BB%E7%B5%B1%E8%A8%93%E7%B7%B4%E6%8C%87%E6%8F%AE%E9%83%A8_-_55521185151.jpg
TAIPEI —
Taiwan's army has put a NT$24.68 million purchase of night-vision and tethered multirotor drones back out to tender, according to a notice posted on the government's e-procurement system on 24 November. Bids close on 8 December and will be opened that afternoon in Taipei.
The notice, issued for the Army Command Headquarters by its logistics command's procurement office, keeps the case number and budget of a first tender published on 16 April. That round, with bids due on 5 May, never reached a contract: a notice dated 20 November said the army would not open or award it because the tender documents had been changed or supplemented, and that it would restart the purchase under the same case number.
Bidders must post a NT$740,000 bid bond and can download the tender papers online, but bids have to be delivered by post or by hand to the logistics command's tender room in Taipei's Nangang district rather than filed electronically, the notice says. The army set 27 November as the deadline for suppliers to raise questions about the documents.

Fixed price, no Chinese parts

The army will pick a supplier through a most-advantageous-tender process, and the winner must deliver within 180 days of the day after the contract is signed, with Tainan named as the place of delivery, the notice shows. The Liberty Times reported that the price is fixed and will not be scored.
According to the paper, the tender rules out drones made in China and parts or raw materials sourced from China, and a local company offering a foreign product must attach the import declaration. The notice does not say how many drones the army wants, nor does it give camera specifications, tether height or flight time, the Liberty Times said.

Watching for hours on a cable

A tethered drone draws power through a cable from equipment on the ground, so it is not limited by battery life the way a normal multirotor drone is, and some systems also pass video and data down the line. That suits long watches over a fixed spot, such as guarding a camp, while night-vision drones carry low-light or infrared thermal cameras to help ground units see in the dark, the Liberty Times said.
The money was set aside in the army's 2026 budget to test whether the drones are worth buying. The Liberty Times reported in August 2025 that the budget plan listed NT$24.675 million for an evaluation of night-vision and tethered drones and a further NT$6.147 million for fibre-optic drones, which are controlled through an optical fibre and so are not affected by electronic jamming.
The paper added that in November 2025 the army asked suppliers to offer 70 training drones and four tethered power modules, which had to have satellite positioning, hovering and automatic return or slow descent, and no Chinese-made parts. It said the army has not explained whether that earlier buy is linked to the new tender.

Taiwan's Navy Tenders NT$36 Billion for 280 VTOL Drones

Bids close 15 December. The notice names no aircraft, but the Navy's budget plan was reported in August as 280 Shield AI V-BATs.
Delfim de Almeida Nov 24, 2026 | 3 min read
Illustration of a generic tail-sitting drone with a ducted fan standing upright on the flight deck of a grey patrol ship, beside a rugged control case
Illustration
Spotted Nov 24, 2026 by FlightBrief's archive , which watches Taiwan's government procurement system, read by FlightBrief's tenders script.
Taiwan’s defence ministry has opened a NT$35.97 billion tender for vertical take-off drones for its navy, about US$1.1 billion. The notice went up on the government procurement system on 16 November, and bids close on 15 December.
It is the largest call on FlightBrief’s list of open drone tenders by some distance. The ministry’s procurement office runs it on behalf of Navy Command and lists the item only as “smart vertical take-off and landing drones”. It names no aircraft and no maker.

What the money buys

The numbers behind the budget sit in the defence ministry’s spending plan for 2027, sent to the Legislative Yuan on 31 August. As reported by the Liberty Times, the programme runs from 2026 to 2029 and costs NT$36.0 billion in all.
It buys 280 drones, 140 control systems and 82 transport vehicles. The navy plans 40 drones this year and 110 in 2027, with NT$13.77 billion set aside for 2027 alone. The last 130 follow in 2028 and 2029.
The plan gives the reason in plain terms. If China ’s opening strikes knock out Taiwan’s command and communications, the navy wants drones that keep watching the sea and resist GPS jamming. They go to its surface combat groups and its littoral forces.

One aircraft in the frame

The tender is open to any qualified firm. When the budget went to the legislature in August, though, United Daily News described the 280 drones as V-BATs, the tail-sitting drone made by the American company Shield AI . The Liberty Times noted that outside attention had focused on the V-BAT, and that the notice does not specify one.
Shield AI already flies in Taiwan. On 13 October it said it had delivered the coast guard’s first V-BAT with Taiwan’s AIDC, under a contract won in July.
The rules favour a maker with a track record. Bidders must prove they have already built or supplied similar equipment, with acceptance records or invoices; a contract alone does not count. Each puts up a NT$50 million bond.
The ministry will choose the most advantageous bid rather than the cheapest, and price counts for at least 20% of the score. Only one firm wins. The purchase is marked as touching national security, and it sits outside Taiwan’s commitments under the WTO’s procurement agreement, so no foreign bidder has a treaty right to compete.

Beside the coast guard’s buy

The scale shows next to the coast guard’s own drone programme. Its officials told legislators in April that it would spend about NT$2.1 billion on 451 vertical take-off drones, Taiwanese papers reported. Its tender for the 18 medium-range drones in that plan, worth NT$782.7 million, closes on 25 November.
The navy is also buying a domestic drone in the same budget. United Daily News reported NT$16.79 billion for 32 Albatross II drones from the National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology, Taiwan’s state weapons laboratory.
The bids for the 280 drones will be opened at the defence ministry in Taipei at 10:00 on 15 December. Unless at least three qualified firms have bid, the ministry will not open them.

Taiwan is investing in autonomous systems, including aerial and sea drones, that have been used widely in the Russia-Ukraine and Iran conflicts. Taiwan recently approved a $7.4 billion drone defense bill, and its military wants to acquire more than 1,400 coastal surveillance and reconnaissance drones, 200,000 attack drones, and 1,320 one-way attack uncrewed surface vessels (USV), the Agence France-Presse (AFP) news agency reported.
Taiwan officials, defense researchers and international companies highlighted the growing importance of uncrewed maritime systems, super intelligence — also known as artificial intelligence — and domestic defense manufacturing during a sea drone exhibition in Taipei in late October 2026. The event showcased how sea drones can monitor around Taiwan, a self-governed island that the Chinese Communist Party threatens to annex by force.
Taipei is prioritizing developing uncrewed systems technologies for economic and strategic reasons. It seeks to supply trusted uncrewed systems to international partners while strengthening Taiwan’s ability to defend itself.
To become a top drone exporter, Taipei must establish three pillars to a domestic industry, officials said at the Taiwan Drone International Forum: forge supply chains that do not involve China; develop and integrate super intelligence into autonomous platforms such as uncrewed aerial vehicles (UAV) to allow decision-making and navigation even during jamming attempts; and finalize international partnerships to allow joint research and development, technology transfers, and collaborative manufacturing.
Demand is spurring the effort. Taiwan exported about 210,000 drones worth $237.6 million between January and July 2026, already surpassing its 2025 total, the Taipei-based CommonWealth Magazine reported.
Taiwan has the expertise and industrial foundation to manufacture sea drones, analysts say, noting electronics manufacturers, precision-machinery suppliers, and motor producers and manufacturers can produce uncrewed systems. Taiwan also is seeking partners to produce battle-tested systems with enhanced software. For instance, the Taiwan Coast Guard plans to buy 25 USVs from United States-based Maritime Tactical Systems that will be manufactured in Taiwan and the U.S.
“If you’ve got a lot of small USVs out there doing a lot of different missions, it really takes a load off of the Coast Guard and the Navy and what some of their gray hull ships are doing,” company executive Seamus Flatley told AFP.
Sea drones, which can be built faster than a warship or submarine, are a relatively low-cost asset that can complicate an adversary’s plans. Global interest in uncrewed underwater vehicles also has soared since the Middle East conflict began in February 2026.

The academy has signed cooperation and training agreements with the Japan Drone Consortium, Palau Community College, the Polish Chamber of Unmanned Systems, Taiwan’s National Chung-Shan Institute of Science and Technology — a military research and development center — and the U.S.-based Association for Uncrewed Vehicle Systems International.

$3,000 a Drone, 10,000-Unit Ceiling: Inside the Army's New 'Manufacturing Rodeo'

The Army wants 400 attack drones built for under $3,000 apiece by March, with the winners earning a shot at scaling to 10,000 units. Here's how the stress test works.

Key Takeaways

* The US Army's 'manufacturing rodeo' solicitation caps vendor drones at $3,000 each for an initial order of 400 Group 1 attack drones.
* Ten percent of each order is due February 15, 2027 for testing, with full delivery of 400 units required by March 1, 2027.
* Vendors that pass the March 2027 Drone Dominance Gauntlet unlock options to scale production to up to 10,000 drones.
* All components must be sourced domestically, with the government providing batteries, motors, lethality kits and frames.
* The program implements acting Army Secretary Adam Telle's 'Affordable Mass' strategy announced in October 2026.
Kaan Tınmaz Nov 19, 2026 Updated Nov 23, 2026
The U.S. Army published a solicitation this week asking vendors to build hundreds of small attack drones for no more than $3,000 each, with the fastest and most reliable builders earning the right to scale into a 10,000-unit production contract. It is less a traditional procurement than a stress test of whether the domestic drone industry can deliver at wartime speed and price.

What exactly is the Army asking vendors to build?

The solicitation, published Monday, November 17, calls for 400 Group 1 one-way attack drones, meaning systems weighing 20 pounds or less, along with 20 ground combat stations per vendor. The Army will supply battery packs, brushless motors, MK118 lethality kits and frame kits as government-furnished equipment, leaving vendors to handle integration, software and final assembly. Every component has to be sourced domestically, with no parts manufactured outside the continental United States.
The program sits under what acting Army Secretary Adam Telle first described in October as a push toward "Affordable Mass," the idea that the service needs thousands of cheap, expendable drones rather than a smaller number of expensive ones, according to Breaking Defense .

Why is the timeline so tight?

Vendors had just two days to submit initial responses after the solicitation dropped. Ten percent of each vendor's order is due by February 15, 2027, for government testing and training, and full delivery of all 400 units is required by March 1, 2027. That compressed schedule is deliberate: the Army wants to see which suppliers can actually move at the pace a contested fight would demand, not just on paper.

What happens to the winners?

Completed systems face off in the Army's third Drone Dominance Gauntlet in March 2027, an event built around complex obstacle courses, heavy electronic jamming and live target arrays. Vendors that clear the gauntlet unlock contractual options for scaled production of up to 10,000 drones, with coproduction lines shared between the vendor and the government rather than run entirely in-house.

Why does this matter beyond one contract?

The $3,000 price cap is the real story. It puts commercial-style manufacturing discipline on a weapons program that has historically tolerated far higher per-unit costs, and it tests whether the mandated all-domestic supply chain can hit that number without the cheap Chinese components that dominate the hobbyist drone market. A failure to hit price or schedule targets would be a signal to the Pentagon that Affordable Mass is harder to execute than to announce. A clean run, on the other hand, gives the Army a template to replicate across other small-drone categories as it tries to close the production gap with adversaries already building attack drones by the thousands.

Indian drone industry says 689 military tenders named Chinese parts, most of them from the Army

Drone Federation India has urged the defence secretary and India's defence chief to bar Chinese drone parts after finding 580 Army tenders that named them.
T
TaiwanDefence
Taipei · 23 Nov 2026, 00:55 TST
2 min read
X Facebook LinkedIn LINE
An Indian Army soldier in a patterned cap watches a US Army soldier holding a drone controller with a tablet screen in scrubland File photo: an Indian Army soldier and a US Army soldier run target drone test flights at Mahajan Field Firing Range, Rajasthan, during exercise Yudh Abhyas on 17 September 2026. Photo: U.S. Army / CW2 MarkAnthony Horak (public domain), via Wikimedia Commons Public domain (US Army work) U.S. Army / Chief Warrant Officer 2 MarkAnthony Horak commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:U_S_,_Indian_Army_Soldiers_conduct_drone_target_test_flights_during_Yudh_Abhyas_2026_(9943981).jpg
TAIPEI —
India's domestic drone industry body has warned the country's top defence officials that hundreds of military purchase tenders asked for Chinese-made drones and drone components, and that the Indian Army issued the large majority of them.
Drone Federation India (DFI) said in a representation dated 20 November, sent to Defence Secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh and Chief of Defence Staff General N S Raja Subramani, that it had found 689 such tenders on the government's online procurement portal, the Government e-Marketplace (GeM), between 10 March 2021 and 19 November 2026.

Army accounts for most tenders

Army units raised 580 of the tenders, or 84 percent, and 328 of the 355 flagged so far in 2026, ThePrint reported. The Border Security Force came a distant second with 12 over the whole period.
The federation said the yearly count rose from 42 in 2024 to 190 in 2025 and then almost doubled again to 355 this year up to 19 November. The Army's own tenders followed the same curve, it said.
According to ThePrint, the bid documents named products from Chinese-linked brands such as EMAX, RunCam, SpeedyBee, T-Motor and GEPRC, covering motors, flight controllers, electronic speed controllers, receivers, cameras and video transmitters. The federation argued that these parts govern a drone's flight, control and data links and are not minor accessories.

Three risks flagged

DFI listed three risks. Parts that units buy for their own use may escape security screening, leaving flight control and data links open to cyber attack. Supplies could be cut off because China began licensing exports of drone motors, speed controllers, autopilots and radios on 18 November. And Indian component makers would lose the demand they need to grow.
The group noted that 104 of this year's flagged Army tenders came after the Army opened its AASHVAST laboratory on 14 August. The facility screens drones for Chinese-origin parts, hidden code and remote-access features before they are cleared for use.
DFI president Smit Shah told Business Standard on Sunday that Army units were asking for Chinese components by name, even though the government banned Chinese parts in military drones in 2023. He said the orders were small and mostly for training and assembly, but argued that the security risk went beyond their size.
The newspaper recalled that the Army cancelled an order for 400 logistics drones in February 2025 after Chinese parts were found in them. It also cited the DFI report as saying that 80 to 90 percent of flight controllers in Indian drones are imported, most of them from China.

Officials point to procurement rules

Defence officials told the Times of India that GeM is a neutral platform on which buyers set specifications but cannot pick a seller or favour a brand. They said Army checks ensure that only compliant products are bought and that a seller caught concealing Chinese components can be blacklisted. ThePrint said the Army had not replied to its request for comment.
The federation has asked for an advisory telling all military formations to exclude Chinese components from drones bought for internal use, a preference for Indian-made critical parts, and mandatory country-of-origin declarations with component-level tracing in future drone bids. It has also requested a meeting with officials.

Brigadier General Matthew Ross, director of JIATF-401, wants systems meeting the evaluation requirements to move rapidly toward purchase orders and increased production. However, no procurement decision resulting from this selection has been announced.

Inside the Drone Interceptor Rush Nobody Is Talking About

Friday, November 20, 2026 By Dylan King news 10 min read
Inside the Drone Interceptor Rush Nobody Is Talking About
The U.S. Army ordered more FD-1 drone interceptors from Mountain Horse Solutions in October 2026 after an initial spring buy, rushing a compact first-person-view (FPV) counter-drone system into European testing before basic questions of cost, scale, and pilot supply were settled.
Press releases love a neat story. A cheaper interceptor arrives, troops test it on a Baltic coast range, and air defense suddenly looks affordable again.
Real defense procurement rarely works that cleanly.
When air defense soldiers with the 5th Battalion, 4th Air Defense Artillery Regiment took the FD-1 drone interceptor to Poland’s Ustka Training Area in early November 2026 under Operation Audacious Fury, they were not celebrating a solved problem. They were trying to figure out how to keep a cheap drone from turning into a training bottleneck, a logistics headache, or an expensive disappointment once massed enemy UAVs start arriving.

The Cost Curve Problem Nobody Can Dodge

Nobody in air defense needs a lecture on why firing million-dollar missiles at cheap drones is a losing game. Look at the math. If an attacker sends dozens or hundreds of Group 1 through Group 3 unmanned aircraft—ranging from small quadcopters to larger fixed-wing platforms—and a defender answers with exquisite surface-to-air missiles, the defender bleeds money even when every single shot connects.
Senior Army leaders have said the quiet part out loud. Then-Army Secretary Dan Driscoll highlighted that cost imbalance in May 2026, and Assistant Secretary of the Army Brent Ingraham echoed the warning at a Pentagon briefing, arguing the service has to stop relying on Patriot missiles to swat down inexpensive drones. Lt. Col. John Verwiel, whose battalion ran the Poland trials, framed the FD-1 drone interceptor around staying on the right side of that cost curve so high-end munitions stay in reserve for targets that actually require them.
That argument makes sense on paper. In practice, cost per shot is only half the equation.
Cost per effective engagement is the real metric. A cheap interceptor that misses half its targets, gets jammed in contested spectrum, or takes three sorties to bring down one hostile drone looks a lot less cheap once you count the airframes consumed and the time lost. Neither the Army nor Mountain Horse Solutions, a subsidiary of Global Ordnance, has publicly disclosed how many FD-1 units were ordered, what the contracts cost, how many interceptors were expended in Poland, or how many targets were actually hit.
Without those numbers, calling the FD-1 drone interceptor a silver bullet is premature. It is an hypothesis under live stress.

How the FD-1 Actually Works

Strip away the buzzwords and the FD-1 is a fast, compact FPV quadcopter built to chase down aerial and ground threats rather than loiter like a reconnaissance drone. According to manufacturer disclosures and defense reporting from the Ustka trials, it can be readied and launched in under two minutes.
Speed is its main calling card. The FD-1 can exceed 265 km/h in its terminal attack phase, with testing reported around 314 km/h. Range depends heavily on configuration—roughly six kilometers in a basic FPV setup, stretching past 20 kilometers with an external antenna.
📖 Related: Why India is Not Buying the US Strategy on Pakistan Anymore
Guidance blends human control with targeted automation.

...

Speed of Buying vs. Speed of Sustainment

One detail from the October 2026 order deserves close scrutiny because it points to a broader shift in how the Pentagon buys gear. Mountain Horse Solutions noted that soldiers evaluated the FD-1, flagged needed improvements, and the company turned updates around in weeks—using a rapid acquisition pathway ( G-TEAD ) without waiting years for a traditional requirements cycle.
Three years ago, that kind of loop between field feedback, software or hardware tweaks, and a follow-on order would have crawled through committees. Getting from initial spring 2026 buy to field assessment to a second order in October 2026 shows real momentum.
* Dimension | Traditional Missile Interceptor | FD-1 FPV Interceptor | Practical Trade-Off
* Per-Shot Cost | High (often millions of dollars) | Lower cost profile, though exact unit price is undisclosed | Cheap interceptors protect budgets against massed drones, provided hit rates stay high.
* Engagement Speed & Reach | Long range and high speed for high-value threats | Fast terminal dash (265+ km/h); ~6 km basic or 20+ km with external antenna | Strong for short-to-medium tactical defense; limited against distant or high-altitude targets.
* Operator & Training Load | Crew-served air defense fire control | Requires FPV pilot skill, sensor cueing, and formal certification | Fast hardware iteration means little if pilot certification lags behind deliveries.

...

What Poland Really Tested

Watching the FD-1 drone interceptor fly over the Baltic coast at Ustka also shows how Central and Eastern Europe have become the proving ground for counter-drone warfare. Poland itself is building out a multi-layered counter-UAS architecture through its SAN air defense program, while U.S. units in Europe have stood up mobile counter-drone teams inspired by lessons from Ukraine.
🔗 Read more: The Whispering Successor and the Geography of Peace
Look closely at what happens when you pair a low-cost FPV interceptor with a Sgt. Stout Stryker and external radar or sensor cueing. A lone FPV pilot hunting blind in wide-open airspace wastes time and battery.

...

If certification takes weeks of dedicated flight hours per soldier, scaling to thousands of interceptors across Europe and beyond will hit a wall.
Third, can domestic manufacturing and allied supply chains keep unit costs low at wartime volumes? Small drones are cheap when built in boutique batches for tests; keeping prices down when thousands are consumed every month requires industrial discipline that many defense suppliers still struggle to sustain.
Watch what the Army does after its trainers finish certifying units across Europe and Africa. If a third or fourth order follows alongside transparent readiness metrics and standardized training tables, the FD-1 drone interceptor will have earned its place in the air defense stack. If quiet silences follow the headlines, we will know the math on the range looked better than the math at scale.

By PJ Simon Nov 24, 2026 · 4:10 a.m. PT
Data center developers facing utility connection waits of up to a decade are opting to build their own off-grid, behind-the-meter gas power plants to fuel artificial intelligence computing, MIT Technology Review reported on Nov. 24, 2026.
As of October 2026, developers have announced plans for more than 100 behind-the-meter gas power plants at facilities in the U.S., according to data from market intelligence firm Cleanview. Those projects total more than 115 gigawatts of planned capacity, more than double California's peak power demand.

...

Shanghai Nexforce Robotics Co., Ltd. (上海新奇机器人有限公司) is a Chinese precision-component maker founded in 2025 and based in Pudong, Shanghai. It supplies core actuation and transmission parts for humanoid robots and embodied-intelligence systems.

NXF-JM integrated joint modules cover harmonic, planetary and cycloidal transmission paths, with stated rotor rotation accuracy below 3 micrometres and torque density up to 300 Nm/kg. NXF-CB micro ceramic ball screws use Si3N4 balls (NSCR0301 / NSCR0401 series, 3-6 mm diameter, C3-C5 accuracy) for dexterous hands. NXF-AB ceramic-ball bearings address satellite solar-array deployment mechanisms, with 9Cr18 rings, Si3N4 balls and PI cages. The company states that several micro ball screws have been validated by Tier-1 suppliers, and that joint modules have gone into lunar-mission special modules, inspection quadrupeds, biopharma and logistics-sorting projects.
